lesson.menu_title: Projections and Deadlines -- Putting a Date on It
lesson.menu_desc: The post-mortem ended with two changes and two dates, and on Tuesday the committee wants the whole plan. Today you learn the three futures English uses to say when -- what you decide in the room, what was already decided, and what is already in the diary -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 19 -- Projections and Deadlines: Putting a Date on It
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Sergio Takashi Tanaka | Lesson 19 -- Projections and Deadlines: Putting a Date on It
lesson.grammar_point: future forms (will, going to, present continuous)

vocabmatch.title: Match the word to its meaning
defs: a fixed point in a plan where one named result has to be finished
the time a plan loses when one step finishes later than planned
not final, and still able to change before the real number arrives
a number for a future period, worked out from what you know today
the work that is waiting and has not been started yet
the time between asking for something and having it ready

listenings.text: Sergio, it is Marina. You are presenting the plan on Tuesday, and there are three things I want in your head before you walk in. First, do not take a plan with one date on it into that room. If the only date is the end, the committee treats the whole thing as one promise, and the first step that slips kills the plan in their eyes. Give them milestones. Four lines, four dates, and then a late step is visible in September instead of in November, which is the entire point of writing it down. Second, and this is the one that gets people into trouble. Never put a date you control and a date another team controls in the same sentence. The room does not hear two owners; it hears one promise, and it is yours. So say the deputy line is closed, that is mine, and then say the alert depends on Risk Systems and their backlog, and give the lead time out loud. Nobody has ever been punished for saying six weeks. People are punished for saying October and arriving in November. Third, the number. If it is not confirmed, call it provisional, and say the day it becomes final. Do not present a provisional figure with a straight face and hope nobody asks, because somebody always asks, and the moment they find out you knew, every other number on your page gets a question mark next to it.

Sergio, Paulo here, from the credit desk. A quick word on how the future sounds in a meeting, because the form you pick tells the room something you may not mean to tell them. Start with going to. When you say we are going to roll it out in September, everyone hears that the decision already exists. It was taken before this meeting, you are reporting it, and the plan is real. That is the strongest thing you can say about a date, and it is why the chair relaxes when she hears it. Then there is will. Will is the decision you make while you are speaking. Someone asks for the number, and you say fine, I will send it on Friday. That is a promise, made right there, and it is perfect for a commitment you are choosing to give in the room. What it is not is a report of an old plan, so do not use it for the rollout. And then the present continuous. I am presenting on Tuesday at nine. That is the diary form, the one people use when the time is booked and somebody else is expecting them, and it lands as the most certain of the three. Last thing, and it is small and it is expensive. Until is not by. Until Friday means the whole week up to Friday. By Friday means not later than Friday, and it can arrive on Tuesday. Every Brazilian I know says until when they mean by, and one day somebody will hold you to it.

extra_audio.text: First, start with the milestones, and put one date next to each of them. Then say which of those dates was decided before the meeting, and which one you are deciding now. Next, give the lead time and the backlog behind the date, so that the room can see the risk. After that, say which date you commit to, and which one you do not commit to yet. Finally, finish with the projection, and name the day the number stops being provisional.
